background.definition: Neck pain is generally called acute if the duration is less than 3 months and chronic if 3 months or more. Uncomplicated or mechanical neck pain is usually considered separately from whiplash associated disorder, defined as neck pain associated with a sudden episode of acceleration-deceleration. Late whiplash syndrome is a constellation of symptoms that continue for more than 6 months after a whiplash injury. Neck pain with radiculopathy is defined as neck pain that is associated with radicular symptoms; usually arm pain or weakness.

list.listitem: Based on the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2017, the incidence of neck pain per 100,000 population ranged from 713.7 to 912.5 (mean 806.6). Estimates were stable from 1990 to 2017.

Although neck pain is common, most adults with neck pain do not see their physician. An estimated 30% to 50% of adults have neck pain at some time during any given year, but only 2% of visits to primary care are for neck pain.

Based on the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study 2017, the point prevalence of neck pain was 3551.1 per 100,000 population. There were no significant differences by gender but prevalence increased by age up to age 70-74 years.
In a meta-analysis of studies of musculoskeletal complaints among hospital physicians, the prevalence of neck pain was 9%-28%.
In a systematic review, the median annual prevalence rate for neck disorders among midwives, nurses, and physicians was 45% compared to 40% for shoulder disorders and 35% for upper back disorders.

In a cross-sectional study of 693 elementary school students in Iran, the prevalence of neck pain was 35.8% and was significantly associated with high desk height, forward or backward seat pan inclination, and too much homework.
In 2016, an estimated $134.5 billion (95% CI, $122.4-$146.9 billion) was spent on low back and neck pain, making these the highest healthcare-spending conditions in the United States.

Whiplash-associated disorder is a major cause of neck pain disability. The annual medical costs associated with whiplash injuries are estimated to range from $3.6 billion in the United Kingdom to $10 billion in the United States.

Global point prevalence for years lived with disability from neck pain per 100,000 population was 352.0 (245.6 to 493.3). These estimates did not change significantly between 1990 and 2017, based on data from the Global Burden of Diseases, Injuries, and Risk Factors Study, 2017.
Based on a telephone survey in Hong Kong, only 1.7% of adults are limited in their ability to do work and 2.4%-11.5% of adults are limited in their social activities.

Patients with chronic neck pain have a statistically significant reduction in respiratory muscle strength and pulmonary function which may be clinically meaningful compared with asymptomatic individuals.
Neck pain is also associated with poorer joint-position sense, oculomotor function, and wider postural sway compared to healthy controls.

Among patients with migraine headache, many report neck pain. Authors of a meta-analysis including 25 clinic-based studies found that no neck pain disability, based on the Neck Disability Index described below, was reported by 23.0%, mild NDI was reported by 45.3%, moderate NDI was reported by 25.0% and severe NDI was reported by 6.7%.

The etiology of neck pain is poorly understood. While injury or trauma is an obvious cause for some, the cause is not identified in many cases and thought to be related to poor posture or "mechanical" in nature.

Authors of a systematic review of 10 cross-sectional studies found that adults with neck pain had increased forward head posture (FHP) but there were negative correlations between FHP and neck pain intensity and disability. There was no association between FHP and most of neck pain measures in adolescents.

There is little evidence that certain jobs, aside from professional sports, cause neck pain. Athletes at particular risk include those who participate in ice hockey, gymnastics, football, wrestling, and auto racing.

In an occupational study of Norwegian workers, the most consistent risk factors for neck pain were role conflict (highest odds ratio [OR] 2.97; 99% CI, 1.29-6.74) and working with arms raised to or above shoulder level (highest OR 1.37; 99% CI, 1.05-1.78), after adjustment for demographics and other confounding exposure factors. The most consistent protective factors were empowering leadership (lowest OR 0.53; 99% CI, 0.35-0.81) and decision control (lowest OR 0.60; 99% CI, 0.36-1.00).
Authors of a meta-analysis found that workplace stressors were associated with a medium increase in neck-shoulder and forearm muscle activity.

In a narrative review of factors associated with neck pain presence and/or severity, authors identified many psychological factors including stress, anxiety, sleep problems, poor social support, and coping strategy (e.g., avoidance-oriented) and work factors including workload (e.g., high demand) and body position (e.g., at computers). Biological factors associated with neck pain included neuromuscular disorders (e.g., cervical spondylosis, fibromyalgia), autoimmune diseases (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, multiple sclerosis), genetic susceptibility (e.g., genetic loci on chromosomes 7 and 17), and gender and age as noted above.
Prevertebral calcific tendinitis is a cause of acute cervical pain that clinically mimics retropharyngeal abscess.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of neck or shoulder trauma

list.listitem: In a 12-month prospective cluster-RCT of 567 healthy office workers with lower-than-normal neck flexion movement or neck flexor endurance, those who were randomized to daily stretching exercise and twice-a-week muscle endurance training had fewer episodes of incident neck pain than control subjects (12.1% vs. 26.7%, respectively).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 RCTs including 1722 participants found exercise interventions reduced the risk of a new neck pain episode (OR 0.5, 95% CI 0.3-0.8) compared to no or minimal intervention at ≤12 months based on moderate-certainty evidence.

In a 3-arm RCT of 193 high-risk office workers in Thailand, new onset neck pain was significantly lower among those randomized to either active breaks or postural shifts compared to control during the 6-month follow-up, occurring in 17%, 17%, and 44% of the participants, respectively.

Use of a dynamic seat cushion that encouraged postural shifts during sitting among high-risk office workers resulted in a reduced incidence of neck (15% vs. 65% in the control group) and low back pain at 6 months in one RCT. However, for individuals experiencing pain, there were no differences between the intervention and control group in pain or disability

In a study of 32 healthy young-adult smartphone users asked to perform texting tasks for three minutes at four different neck flexion angles, the lowest gravitational moment of the neck at 0° flexion was consistent with the lowest CES muscle activity and the lowest neck discomfort score; advice on non-flexed head positioning may help reduce neck pain.

In a feasibility study of 24 patients presenting to the emergency department with whiplash injury of <48 hours who were at high-risk of poor recovery based on initial pain scores >4/10, pregabalin 75 mg twice daily titrated to 300 mg twice daily for 1 month appeared to reduce pain intensity at 3 and 6 months compared to placebo, but not at 12 months. Minor adverse events were more common with pregabalin.
Initial evaluation should consist of a careful history and physical exam. Have a high index of suspicion in patients with a history of malignancy or other signs of malignancy. C
Suspect metastatic malignancy in patients with neck pain and an elevated ESR or lytic lesions on neck radiographs. B

C For patients with acute or increasing cervical pain without radiculopathy, radiography of cervical spine may be appropriate. When there is suspected or known infection or a diagnosis of malignancy in patients with acute or increasing cervical pain or radiculopathy, MRI without and with contrast is usually appropriate and CT without or with contrast may be considered. Lytic lesions on x-ray and high ESR, with history of cancer or unexplained weight loss; significant bony tenderness on exam
Immunosuppression, previous spine surgery, history of intravenous drug abuse (IVDA), prolonged steroid use
Fever, neck stiffness, photophobia, focal neurologic signs, rash
Morning stiffness improves with exercise, other joints affected, elevated ESR, may have positive rheumatoid factor
Radicular weakness, numbness, decreased dexterity, paresthesias of arms, reduced deep tendon reflexes, deep neck aching

list.listitem: Ask about onset and duration of pain. Is there a relationship of pain onset to trauma, new physical activity, or increased intensity of a usual activity? Is there any radiation of the pain? Has the patient had this pain in the past, and if so, how long did it last and what treatment was effective?

Ask about a history of malignancy or weight loss. Also ask about any history of osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis (fragility fracture), spine surgery, immunosuppression, and IVDA, or prolonged steroid use (infection). Patients with Down syndrome are at risk of subluxation from atlantoaxial ligament laxity.
Ask about paresthesias, weakness, or clumsiness. Also ask about any other neurologic problems, such as bowel and bladder dysfunction, gait disturbance, or electric shocks going down spine.

Based on a qualitative analysis of 9 studies, patient experiences with neck pain include physical concerns, psychological consequences (e.g., worry, coping) and social concerns (e.g., influences on work, activities of daily living). Addressing these concerns may improve care of patients with neck pain.

In a study of 200 patients evaluated for suspected cervical or lumbosacral nerve root compression, dermatomal pain was the most sensitive predictor and segmental reflex loss and myotomal weakness were the most specific individual predictors of nerve root disease.

The Spurling test provides limited evidence for cervical nerve impingement from disc herniation. It is done by having the patient flex the neck laterally and extend the neck, then the examiner exerts a downward pressure on the head, compressing the neck. A positive test results in the patient having radicular pain. A negative test does not rule out radiculopathy.

Authors of two systematic reviews found the craniocervical flexion test to be valid and reliable for use in clinical practice as an assessment of the deep neck flexor muscle strength/endurance, and to identify patients with nonspecific neck pain who might benefit from a targeted intervention. This test is performed with the patient supine and a blood pressure cuff placed under the neck and slowly inflated by the patient from 20 to 30 mm Hg, stopping every 2 mm Hg and having the patient tuck the chin and hold the position for 10 seconds then rest for 30 seconds. Failure to hold the position from 26-30 mm Hg is a positive test.

Based on a review of 31 studies, the best measures of cervical muscle strength were the craniocervical flexion test, cervical flexor and extensor endurance test, and cervical muscle strength using a handheld dynamometer; these tests showed moderate to good intra- and interrater reliability (intraclass correlation coefficients ranging from 0.64-0.90).

In patients with trauma, individual signs and symptoms are of limited value. Midline neck tenderness is the single most helpful finding to rule in or rule out cervical spine fracture. Combinations of signs and symptoms are more useful (see Clinical Decision Rules section). The combination of midline neck tenderness or intoxication or altered level of consciousness or severely painful injury identified all patients with cervical spine fracture in one study.

Authors of a retrospective study of 1035 elderly patients seen in the emergency department following a ground-level fall, found a combination of evidence of external trauma above the clavicles, C-spine tenderness, and altered mental status had a sensitivity of 100% and specificity of 40.0% for detection of cervical fracture (identified in 16 [1.5%] patients).
In patients with whiplash, reduced total cervical range of motion predicts disability 1 year later.

Smartphone applications, including clinometer and compass apps, showed sufficient intra-rater reliability, inter-rater reliability, and validity to be used for measuring neck range of motion in people with and without neck pain, based on low-quality evidence.

The Neck Disability Index (NDI) is a tool for assessing and monitoring disability in patients with neck pain. Authors of a Japanese web-based study found that the best cut-off value of the NDI to detect neck pain associated with disability was 15. NDI scores range from 0 to 50; 0–4 points signify no disability, 5–14 points mild disability, 15–24 points moderate disability, 25–34 points severe disability and scores of ≥ 35 points indicate complete disability. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis including 79 studies of which 70 were considered at low risk of bias concluded that the NDI demonstrated good internal consistency and test-retest reliability without floor or ceiling effect.
Initial imaging in patients with acute traumatic pain should be guided by the NEXUS or Canadian rules (see below).

Initial imaging in patients with acute nontraumatic pain is only recommended for patients with radicular symptoms, primarily if progressive over 3-4 weeks, red flags are present as listed below, or if unimproved with conservative treatment.

The American College of Radiology (ACR, 2024) states that cervical spine radiographs or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without contrast may be appropriate for patients with chronic neck pain or for those with acute or increasing cervical pain with radiculopathy. For patients with acute or increasing cervical pain without radiculopathy, radiography of cervical spine may be appropriate. When there is suspected or known infection or a diagnosis of malignancy in patients with acute or increasing cervical pain or radiculopathy, MRI without and with contrast is usually appropriate and CT without or with contrast may be considered. For patients who have had prior cervical surgery and experience acute or increasing cervical pain or radiculopathy, radiography of cervical spine, MRI without contrast or CT without contrast are usually appropriate.

If there is concern about cancer based on onset over age 50 years, history of cancer, weight loss, or other risk factors, then order a sedimentation rate and radiographs. Sedimentation rate over 50 mm/hour (and especially over 100 mm/hour) and/or lytic lesions on radiographs are highly suggestive of malignancy. These data largely come from studies of patients with lower back pain but also apply to cervical spine pathology.

In patients with prior cervical spine surgery and new or increasing non-traumatic neck pain or radiculopathy, ACR recommends radiography of the cervical spine or computed tomographyt (CT) of the cervical spine without IV contrast as initial imaging. If infection is suspected, an MRI cervical spine without and with IV contrast is appropriate.
CT findings in patients with prevertebral calcific tendinitis show calcium deposits in the right longus colli muscle.

The North American Spine Society guidelines on Diagnosis and Treatment of Cervical Radiculopathy and Degenerative Disorders (2011) found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against use of electromyography for patients in whom the diagnosis of cervical radiculopathy is unclear after clinical exam and MRI.
Initial imaging for a patient with chronic neck pain is cervical spine radiographs for all patients (ACR 2024).

Authors of a retrospective study found that the extension radiograph was the most sensitive for predicting the severity of cervical disc degeneration and disc protrusion using MRI as the standard. The radiograph of C5/6 had the highest sensitivity (93.33%) and specificity (100%) although segmental horizontal displacement at C3/4, C4/5, and C5/6 level had a significant correlation with MRI severity of cervical disc degeneration.

If initial radiographs are normal in a patient with chronic neck pain and the patient has neurologic symptoms or the radiographs show bone or disc margin destruction, MRI of the cervical spine is recommended (ACR 2024). A CT of the cervical spine without IV contrast may be appropriate.

There are two validated clinical decision rules to guide radiographic decision making about patients with acute traumatic neck pain. Both the Canadian Cervical spine rule and NEXUS rule identify patients at very low risk for cervical spine injury, who do not require radiographs.

Although NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and muscle relaxants are widely recommended, there is little evidence from RCTs of benefit.

Topical diclofenac diethylamine (DDEA) 1.16% gel was more effective than placebo for pain on movement at 48 hours in an RCT of 72 patients with acute neck pain; response to treatment was 94.4% vs. 8.3%, respectively.

Topical lidocaine patch demonstrated a trend of improvement in neck pain over placebo patch in a cross-over RCT including 76 patients; 27.7% of patients experienced a pain reduction versus 14.9% during the placebo phase (P=0.07).

In an RCT evaluating opioid analgesia for acute low back pain and neck pain among 347 adults, there were no differences between opioid, dosed twice daily, or placebo in the primary outcome of pain at 6 weeks. Treatment continued until the pain score was 0 or 1 out of 10 for 3 consecutive days or for a maximum of 6 weeks.
For acute whiplash, IV methylprednisolone given within 8 hours improved pain at 1 week and reduced sick leave at 6 months.

A single intracutaneous injection of lidocaine, bupivacaine and methylprednisolone was more effective than ibuprofen in patients with acute nonspecific neck pain with respect to pain and neck disability in a small RCT of 36 patients.

Authors of a meta-analysis of pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions for chronic neck pain found no benefit of anti-inflammatory drugs alone or in combination with another non-pharmacological treatment on pain at 1 month or 3 to 6 months.
Topical capsaicin 0.1% was no more effective then placebo hydrogel patch in an RCT of 61 patients with chronic myofascial neck pain.
Intramuscular lidocaine was more effective than placebo (NNT = 3) and similar in effectiveness to ultrasound in patients with chronic neck pain.

In patients with chronic myofascial neck pain, Cochrane authors found low quality evidence of an effect in pain for intramuscular local anesthetic injection vs. control and for nerve block with anesthetic over saline. There was moderate quality evidence suggesting little or no difference in pain or function and disability between nerve block injection of steroid and bupivicaine vs. bupivicaine alone for chronic neck pain.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs with 370 patients with chronic neck pain also found no differences between cervical epidural injection with steroid plus local anesthetic vs. local anesthetic only with respect to pain and functional scores.
In patients with chronic neck pain and radiculopathy, epidural methylprednisolone and lidocaine were more effective than intramuscular dosing in one study.

Botulinum toxin is not effective for chronic musculoskeletal neck pain based on five high-quality trials. However, in cases of cervical dystonia, defined as involuntary, painful neck muscle contraction causing painful head posturing, authors of a Cochrane review of 9 RCTs (of which 7 excluded patients with poorer response to treatment) concluded that a single botulinum toxin type A injection results in a clinically-relevant reduction of cervical dystonia-specific impairment and pain. The most common treatment-related side effects were neck weakness (14%), dysphagia (11%), and diffuse weakness or tiredness (8%).

The authors of an international evidence-based practice guideline strongly recommend against the use of corticosteroid and/or local anesthetic injections or radiofrequency ablation for chronic low back or cervical spine pain not related to cancer. These recommendations are based on systematic reviews and a network meta-analysis of RCTs that found no evidence that these treatments provide benefits beyond placebo.

Disectomy with or without fusion is an option for patients with cervical degenerative disc disease. Operative treatment was superior to non-surgical management for patients with moderate to severe myelopathy in two cohort studies. Nonoperative treatment is likely equivalent or better than surgery in those with mild myelopathy.
In a meta-analysis of class III studies, posterior C1-2 fusion was found to be safe and effective with respect to intractable neck pain for patients with lateral atlantoaxial osteoarthritis.

Use of bone morphogenetic protein (BMP) as an osteoinductive agent commonly used in lumbar fusion was evaluated in a meta-analysis including 20 studies with 5828 patients undergoing cervical arthrodesis. In ACDF cases, addition of BMP was associated with higher fusion rates (98.9% vs 93.6%), lower reoperation rates (2.2% vs 3.1%), but higher risk of dysphagia (24.7% vs 8.1%). In posterior cervical fusion cases, BMP was not associated with significant differences in fusion or reoperation rates but was associated with significantly higher blood loss during surgery.

Use of preoperative, ultrasound-guided selective nerve root block was a useful test for determining the appropriate level for discectomy among patients with multilevel cervical disease. In this RCT, patients undergoing nerve root block followed by surgery had significantly lower VAS scores for pain intensity than control post-surgical patients with more patients reporting ≥50% reduction in their pain scores from baseline at four, eight, and 12 weeks that control patients.

In a follow-up study of 73 patients (77% of the original sample) who were at least 10 years after ACDF, most (75%) reported no clinically relevant improvement in neck-specific disability and 43% had no relevant improvement in pain intensity. Predictive factors of good outcome after ACDF were initial high neck-related pain intensity, nonsmoking status at the time of surgery, and male gender.

For patients with cervical myelopathic spondylosis, authors of a systematic review found laminoplasty (decompression, lamina hinged-open but not removed) and laminectomy and fusion procedures similarly effective, although data were inconsistent. Reoperation rates appeared lower after laminoplasty, but the incidence of debilitating neck pain was higher. In a more recent meta-analysis of 14 studies, authors confirmed similar outcomes between the two procedures with the exception that laminectomy with fusion resulted in higher rates of total complications (OR 2.60, 95% CI 1.85-3.64) and nerve palsies (OR 3.18, 95% CI 1.66-6.11).

For patients undergoing discectomy, local steroid application was effective in reducing neck pain or odynophagia and length of hospital stay by about 1 day and mitigated prevertebral soft tissue swelling and dysphagia in the early postoperative period.

listitem.strong: Cervical disc arthroplasty (disc replacement) with or without anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF)

list.listitem: Authors of a systematic review identified 4 RCTs that directly compared surgical treatments for cervical radiculopathy. Three compared ACDF with cervical disc replacement, while one compared ACDF with minimally invasive posterior cervical discectomy. All were similarly effective, with cervical disc replacement requiring the least second surgical procedures and minimally invasive posterior discectomy having the fewest complications and adverse events.

In one metaanalysis of 10 trials, cervical disc arthroplasty resulted in better mean neck disability indexes, reduced incidence of reoperation related to the index surgery at 1-5 years, and reduced rates of major surgical complications compared to ACDF. A second meta-analysis had similar findings for 8 RCTs comparing cervical disc arthroplasty with ACDF.

In another metaanalysis of 27 RCTs, ACDF was associated with shorter operative times and less blood loss compared with arthroplasty with equivalent rates of length of hospital stay, Neck Disability Index (NDI) scores, and rates of adverse events and reoperations.

At a minimum of 4 years of follow-up, total disc arthroplasty showed improvements over ACDF in disability, scores of neck and arm pain, and SF-36 physical components based on a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs.

In a 5-year follow-up of patients with C6 or C7 radiculopathy enrolled in an RCT comparing arthroplasty to anterior discectomy and fusion, at 5-year follow-up (N=114/136, 83.8%), mean NDI scores significantly improved in both groups and there were no differences between groups in mean change in disability score, arm or neck pain, or patients requiring re-operation (10 patients [14.7%] vs 8 patients [11.8%], respectively).

At a minimum of 7-years follow up, cervical disc arthroplasty was superior to ACDF in overall success rate and improvement in NDI and VAS arm pain based on a meta-analysis of 9 RCTs with 2664 patients.

A 10-year follow-up of an RCT comparing cervical disc arthroplasty with anterior cervical discectomy and fusion found a trend toward lower likelihood of adjacent level degeneration with arthroplasty (10% vs 16%, p = 0.15). Cervical disc arthroplasty devices may be superior to ACDF in reducing the risk of adjacent segment degeneration as well as the need for further surgeries.

In a small follow-up study at 20 years for 43 of 47 original patients with single-level cervical radiculopathy, cervical disk arthroplasty was equivalent to ACDF in sustained improvement in NDI scores, VAS neck and VAS arm pain. Those undergoing disk arthroplasty, however, had lower reoperation rates (10% vs. 41.7%, respectively).

In a meta-analysis of 2 prospective and 5 retrospective trials, hybrid surgery (artificial cervical disc arthroplasty with fusion) achieved better recovery of NDI score at 2-years compared to ACDF for the treatment of multilevel cervical spondylosis and disc diseases.

Hybrid surgery was found to be similar to ACDF on symptom improvement, clinical outcomes and complication rates in the most recent systematic review and meta-analysis of 17 studies involving 861 patients with multilevel cervical disc degeneration.

In an RCT of 209 patients randomized to cervical total disc replacement with ProDisc-C or ACDF, both groups had significant improvement at 2 and 5 years over baseline. Patients in the ProDisc-C group had statistically significantly less neck pain intensity and frequency and a significantly lower rate of reoperation compared with ACDF patients (2.9% vs. 11.3%).
Cervical disc arthroplasty devices may be superior to ACDF in reducing the risk of adjacent segment degeneration as well as the need for further surgeries.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 primarily retrospective studies including 486 patients with unilateral cervical radiculopathy without myelopathy found posterior endoscopic cervical foraminotomy successful based on improvements in visual-analog neck and arm scores and NDI score. Complication rates with this procedure were lower than reported for ACDF although the proportion of patients requiring reoperation was similar between the two procedures.

A meta-analysis of 9 non-RCTs demonstrated high success rates in treatment of cervical disc herniation with percutaneous endoscopic cervical discectomy for relief of neck pain from baseline, with low rates of recurrence (3%) and incidence of adverse events (5%).

Cohorts undergoing minimally invasive posterior cervical foraminotomy had similar outcomes compared to ACDF cohorts with respect to operation time, complication and reoperation rates, neck and arm pain, and NDI scores in a meta-analysis of 7 studies with 1175 patients. Patients undergoing the minimally invasive procedure were discharged from hospital sooner.

Two-year results from an RCT including 265 patients with single-level cervical radiculopathy comparing posterior cervical foraminotomy to anterior discectomy with fusion demonstrated noninferiority for success rate based on the Odom criteria and arm pain reduction.

In patients with symptomatic cervical radiculopathy, both minimally invasive posterior cervical foraminotomy and the anterior transcorporeal approach appear comparable for complications and reoperation rates based on a meta-analysis of 40 studies including 1661 patients, although the anterior approach had greater improvement in VAS neck pain scores.
Sternocleidomastoid release led to functional improvement and pain relief for adults with congenital muscular torticollis in one case series. There were no associated serious complications.

There is some evidence for the efficacy of radiofrequency ablation. In one systematic review, authors found Level II evidence for long-term effectiveness of radiofrequency neurotomy and facet joint nerve blocks in managing cervical facet joint pain.

In patients with chronic axial pain of facet joint origin, authors of a series of meta-analyses found facet joint nerve blocks effective for pain relief compared to local anesthesia controls at 3 and 6 months but not 12 months, based on 3 RCTs.

The 2009 National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guideline developers, however, found little supporting evidence on safety and efficacy of percutaneous endoscopic laser cervical discectomy. They advise patient education about this uncertainty and referral to a clinician with specific training in the use of lasers and in endoscopy of the spinal canal.

Yoga therapy may be effective in reducing neck pain, disability, and quality of life although authors of this meta-analysis of 10 small RCTs noted difficulty in combining studies due to different session and duration of the yoga interventions and different outcome measures.

Both chiropractic spinal manipulation and extensive education about home exercise (two 1-hour sessions of instruction) were more effective than standard treatment with medication in decreasing symptoms in patients with mechanical neck pain.

Cochrane authors found multiple sessions of cervical manipulation to have similar benefit to multiple sessions of cervical mobilization for pain and quality of life for patients with acute and chronic neck pain and to be better than some medications and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS). Thoracic manipulation was found to improve pain in participants with acute and subacute neck pain and function in patients with acute and chronic neck pain, although there was evidence of publication bias.

Osteopathic interventions compared to no intervention or sham treatment for adults with non-specific neck pain appeared to be effective for pain and functional status based on low-quality evidence from 4 RCTs. Authors of a meta-analysis of 28 RCTs found very low to low certainty evidence that spinal manipulation in patients with recent and persistent nonspecific neck pain reduced pain and disability.

Thoracic manipulation in patients with neck pain resulted in reduced pain and disability and improved quality of life and range of motion without serious side effects based on a meta-analysis of 18 RCTs including 914 participants.

Based on a meta-analysis of 6 studies, there is moderate to very low certainty evidence that there is no difference in effectiveness between cervical thrust or non-thrust manipulations and thoracic or cervicothoracic manipulations for improving pain, disability, and range of motion in patients with neck pain. In another meta-analysis of 14 articles of cervical manipulation, authors found no moderate or serious adverse effects resulting from high-velocity, low-amplitude cervical manipulation over various control interventions.

Among patients with tension-type headache and neck pain, manipulation plus exercise was superior to suboccipital inhibition plus exercise (myofascial release), and exercise only on headache frequency, pain severity and headache and neck disability in a 3-arm RCT with 45 patients.

Among patients with chronic neck pain, modest effects were seen for pain reduction and range of motion for myofascial release based on a meta-analysis of 10 RCTs including 549 patients, and for reduction in pain intensity and disability for manipulative therapy based on a meta-analysis of 17 RCTs with 1190 participants.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs with 395 patients diagnosed with cervicogenic cephalic syndrome (cervicogenic headache and dizziness due to cervical joint dysfunction) found that patients who underwent manual therapy (either high or low-velocity) compared to sham or placebo treatment showed lower NDI scores and better cervical spine range of motion but no difference in frequency of cervicogenic cephalic syndrome episodes. No serious adverse effects were reported.
In 1 small Spanish RCT, manual therapy and TENS were both effective for short-term relief of neck pain in 50% of patients, decreasing to one-third at 6 month follow-up.

Evidence-based practice positions were developed by an international task force using a literature review and Delphi process regarding spinal manipulation use in children. They concluded that it may be appropriate to treat musculoskeletal conditions including spinal mobility impairments associated with neck-back pain and neck pain with headache using spinal mobilization and manipulation on adolescents, spinal mobilization on children or thoracic manipulation on children for neck-back pain only.

Ischemic compression of myofascial trigger points was effective in immediate and short-term pain intensity reduction and increased range of motion in patients with neck pain based on a meta-analysis of 15 studies including 725 patients.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs of patients with chronic neck pain conducted outside the U.S. found little and low-certainty evidence of any difference between TENS and sham TENS on reducing neck pain.
While research is not of high quality, there is some evidence from RCTs that acupuncture is effective for neck pain and whiplash injury (for pain reduction and range of motion).

In an RCT of 236 patients with acute musculoskeletal pain of the neck, back, arms, or legs presenting to the emergency department, those randomized to receive 20 to 30 minutes of either auricular (“battlefield”) acupuncture or peripheral acupuncture to various body sites at the discretion of the acupuncturist had a clinically important difference in pain scores at 1 hour after treatment compared to a control group receiving no adjunctive treatment.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 10 RCTs including 754 patients found acupuncture superior to conventional treatment for patients with stiff neck in total effective rate, reducing VAS scores, reducing NDI scores and restoring cervical range of motion. A sham acupuncture group would have been helpful to rule out a placebo effect.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs of patients with persistent head and neck myofascial pain found a 19-point difference (95 %CI: -29.13 to -8.95) in pain intensity between acupuncture and sham-needling/no intervention, with high levels of safety as evidenced by low rates of side effects or treatment withdrawal.

For patients with chronic neck pain, both acupuncture and sham acupuncture as adjunct therapy appeared to provide post-treatment pain relief lasting at least 3 months based on a meta-analysis of 18 RCTs.

Electroacupuncture vs. biofeedback twice weekly for a total of 6 sessions as an adjunct to conventional treatment was evaluated in an RCT of 50 patients with chronic neck pain diagnosed with cervical myofascial pain syndrome. The primary outcome of a 20% reduction in the 3-month neck pain and dysfunction compared to baseline was achieved in more patients in the acupuncture group (20 vs. 10 patients).

In a RCT of 517 patients with nonspecific chronic neck pain, both treatment groups - acupuncture sessions or Alexander Technique lessons – had significant reductions in neck pain and associated disability compared with usual care at 12 months. Among patients with chronic nonspecific neck pain, the Alexander technique was more effective than conventional therapy for short-term pain relief based on 2 RCTs and one quasi-experimental study.

In one study, 177 patients with chronic neck pain were randomized to acupuncture, sham acupuncture with a laser, or massage. Acupuncture was more effective than massage, but so was laser, throwing the results into doubt.

In a series of network meta-analyses of 65 RCTs with 5266 participants with neck pain evaluating 9 interventions, investigators concluded that fire (hot needle) acupuncture, electroacupuncture, and warm acupuncture were more effective than manual acupuncture for pain intensity reduction and efficacy rate; electroacupuncture also decreased pain-related disability more than manual acupuncture.

Data on the effects of dry needling for neck pain are conflicting. Authors of a meta-analysis of 6 RCTs with 241 patients found dry needling and trigger point manual therapy similarly effective for pain and function among patients with myofascial pain syndrome of the neck and upper back. In another meta-analysis of 6 trials comparing these two therapies, authors concluded a superior effect for trigger point injection compared to dry needling for decreasing pain of cervical muscles in the short term.

Dry needling was effective in patients with chronic neck pain for improvements in cervical pain and/or disability based on 14 clinical trials for qualitative analysis and 13 for quantitative analysis.

In an RCT of 77 adults referred to physical therapy with acute, subacute, or chronic mechanical neck pain, the addition of trigger point dry needling to manual therapy and exercise did not further reduce pain or disability, which improved in both groups at 1 and 6 months and 1 year. However, authors of a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs found dry needling combined with other interventions reduced pain intensity at short-term and midterm, but not immediately after or at long-term compared with the other interventions alone, based on low to moderate evidence. They also found a small effect on short-term pain-related disability.

Authors of a systematic review found dry needling for patients with neck pain with trigger points in the upper trapezius muscle had a positive effect on pain intensity greater than active range of motion exercises or placebo intervention or usual care, but similar to other therapeutic approaches. However, in the most recent RCT of 101 patients with chronic mechanical neck pain, those randomized to two sessions of dry needling of the most mechano-sensitive myofascial trigger point in addition to manual therapy had significantly lower pain intensity, pain pressure threshold, neck range of motion, and neck disability index scores than the sham dry needling and manual therapy group at 4 weeks.

Combination acupuncture and intradermal needling was superior to either acupuncture alone or sham acupuncture on pain and some quality-of-life scores in an RCT of 896 adults with chronic neck pain from cervical spondylosis.

In a small RCT, a single Gua sha treatment (an East Asian healing technique where the body surface is press-stroked with a smooth-edged instrument to intentionally raise therapeutic petechiae) was more effective for pain relief (−29.9 mm; 95% CI, −43.3 to −16.6 mm) and function at one week than a heating pad treatment.
There is low quality evidence from 2 RCTs of Chinese herbal medicine that compound Qishe tablets relieved pain better in the short term than either placebo or Jingfukang.

Authors of a systematic review of 57 studies found that Chinese medicine outperformed Western medicine for analgesic effect in patients with neck and low back pain with no significant side effects reported.

Physiotherapy interventions using a multimodal approach and/or active strengthening exercises appear to produce the most benefit with respect to strength, function, health-related quality of life, and reduced pain. Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis including 22 studies found a multi-modal treatment approach including exercise and manual therapy had similar effects to manual therapy alone, but was more effective than exercise alone or other interventions for treatment of nonspecific neck pain and related disability.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 32 pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions for chronic neck pain based on 119 RCTs with 12,496 patients found that a combination of active and/or passive multimodal non-pharmacological inventions (e.g., exercise and manual therapy) were effective for improving pain and disability at 3 to 6 months. Other authors found isometric and range-of-motion exercises exerted a hypoalgesia effect at local and remote sites for patients with neck pain.

Strengthening, stretching, isometric, and eye-fixation exercises are effective for treatment of neck disorders. Specific neck exercises targeting deep cervical flexors and extensors may be more effective for reducing pain and disability than alternate exercise interventions for treatment of non-specific neck pain based on a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs. Other authors also found positive effects on pain and disability for various exercise types, but no optimal exercise intervention for patients with chronic neck pain.

For whiplash injury, authors of a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs found that guided neck-specific exercise therapy provided greater benefits in reduced pain and disability than a different or unguided neck-specific exercise therapy, primarily for intervention periods of more than 6 weeks with at least two sessions per week.

In an RCT including 76 patients with chronic neck pain, the combination of McKenzie exercises (which use backward and forward bending movements) plus stabilization exercises resulted in significantly greater reduction in current neck pain intensity compared to McKenzie alone at 6 weeks. Neck disability improved in both groups.
Neck strengthening and workplace modification are effective at reducing neck pain in office workers based on a meta-analysis of 29 trials.

Neural mobilization, gentle nerve stretching, in the management of musculoskeletal neck disorders appears to be effective for improving overall pain intensity, neck rotation and disability when embedded in a physiotherapy treatment compared to no intervention, but is not superior when compared to other types of treatment.
In a small RCT, qigong was equivalent to exercise and better than no treatment for patients with chronic neck pain.

In an RCT of 139 patients with nonspecific neck pain, adding aerobic exercise to 6 weeks of neck-specific exercises was more effective than neck-specific exercise alone in reducing neck pain, disability and headache at 6 months compared to baseline.
Interestingly, in a systematic review of exercise therapy vs. no-exercise therapy, exercise dosage parameters did not predict pain or disability.
A high-quality study of mechanical traction found no evidence of benefit.
Evidence regarding physical therapy and other conservative treatments for whiplash is inconsistent and of poor quality.
Exercise programs were effective in relieving chronic whiplash-related pain and disability over the short term; 2 RCTs on interdisciplinary interventions provided conflicting results.
In a RCT of 172 patients with chronic pain from whiplash, 30 minutes of brief advice was as effective with respect to pain scores as 20 individualized comprehensive sessions with a physiotherapist.

In another RCT of patients with chronic whiplash-associated neck pain, investigators found physiotherapist-led neck-specific exercise with or without a behavioral approach was better, with respect to general disability and most psychological factors, than prescribed physical activity at two-year follow-up.

Similar findings were reported in an RCT 188 patients with chronic whiplash-associated disorders and headache randomized to 12 weeks of neck-specific exercise with or without a behavioral approach vs. a physical activity prescription. Half to 61% of patients in the two intervention groups reported at least a 50% reduction in their headache at 12 months compared to none in the activity-prescription group.
Normal activities are associated with a better outcome than neck braces in whiplash injury.

With respect to exercise for mechanical neck disorders, low to moderate quality evidence supports use of specific cervical and scapular stretching and strengthening exercise for improving short and intermediate-term chronic neck pain. There was no benefit for some upper extremity stretching and strengthening exercises or a general exercise program on these disorders.

In an RCT of 64 patients, 2 sessions of Pilates per week for 12 weeks resulted in improved pain, function, and SF-36 scores and less use of acetaminophen than a control group up to 6 months post intervention.

For work-related complaints of the arm, neck or shoulder, authors of a systematic review found primarily low quality evidence indicating no benefit on multiple outcomes for specific exercises. Ergonomic interventions led to long-term pain reduction but no difference at short-term follow-up and behavioral interventions had inconsistent effects on pain and disability.
The combination of mobilization and/or manipulation combined with exercise is effective for patients with mechanical neck pain; no long-term data are available.

No conservative intervention is clearly beneficial for patients with cervical radiculopathy and most patients improve over time. However, in a small RCT of men with chronic radicular cervical pain, a hypolordotic cervical spine, and anterior head translation posture, those randomized to use of the Denneroll cervical traction device in addition to multimodal therapy had lower intensity neck and arm pain and less disability at one year.
There is very little research on biopsychosocial rehabilitation for chronic neck pain.

Cochrane authors did not find cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for subacute neck pain to be better than placebo for clinically significant pain relief or improvement of disability. For patients with chronic neck pain, CBT appeared effective for pain relief and in improving disability over placebo but the degree of improvement was of unclear clinical importance and the study quality was poor.

Other authors found low certainty evidence suggesting a clinically significant pain reduction (short-term) favoring CBT with or without additional intervention compared to no intervention for patients with chronic neck pain.

A nurse-managed, home-based telemedicine intervention following outpatient rehabilitation in patients with chronic neck pain increased adherence to home exercise and reduced pain and disability more at 6-month follow-up in one RCT compared to an advice-only control group (pain reduction and disability reduction also seen).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 60 RCTs found that placebo produced a mean improvement in pain of 15.6 (Mean Difference [MD] -15.6, 95% CI -19.19, -12.12) compared to no treatment (MD -5.80, 95% CI 13.28, 1.69) and active treatment (MD -25.91, 95% CI -29.15, -22.68). They calculated that placebo effect accounted for 38% of the pain score improvement in active intervention groups.

Authors of a Cochrane review found educational nterventions to be ineffective for neck pain. However, combining pain neuroscience education plus exercise compared with exercise alone reduced VAS pain after treatment and at 3 months and reduced functional disability in patients with neck pain based on a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs including 246 patients.
Workplace interventions may reduce sick leave at 6 months (but not at 3 months or 12 months).

Optimizing sleep position may be helpful. Recommend an anatomically neutral head position if the patient sleeps on their left or right side, and consider a foam mattress and/or pillow for greater support.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 high-quality studies with 555 participants with chronic neck pain found use of spring and rubber (latex) pillows were effective in reducing neck pain, waking symptoms, and neck disability.

Use of a dynamic seat cushion improved recovery rate from neck and/or low back pain over a control group using a placebo seat pad in an RCT including 66 office workers; probability of recovery was higher (HRadj 4.4, 95% CI 1.9-10.1) and recurrence rate was lower (27% and 75%, respectively) in the intervention group.

Dynamic taping as an adjunct to standard physiotherapy yielded improved pain levels, functional disability, and well-being among patients with chronic non-specific neck pain compared to the sham group for the duration of the taping.

Virtual reality was shown to reduce pain intensity for patients with neck pain with a standardized mean difference of -0.51 (95% CI -0.91 to -0.11) compared with controls based on moderate quality evidence from 8 studies including 382 participants. It is thought that virtual reality works by distraction from pain.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 15 RCTs with 990 patients with neck pain found benefit of biofeedback on reducing neck pain disability in the short- and intermediate-term, but no effect on pain or work ability.

Chinese mind-body exercise had a positive effect on neck range of motion in patients with neck pain based on a meta-analysis of 4 studies with 208 patients. However, authors of a second meta-analysis of 6 studies with 716 patients concluded that there was insufficient evidence to support this treatment for improving pain intensity, functional mobility or QOL in individuals with neck pain.

In an RCT, both heat and cold application for 30 minutes decreased pain similarly when given with 400 mg of oral ibuprofen to patients presenting to an emergency department (ED) with a complaint of back or neck pain of less than 24 hours duration resulting from a minor injury.
In an RCT of 20 patients with nonspecific neck pain, local heat applied to trigger points significantly better than sham treatment on pain relief.

A meta-analysis of massage for neck pain found that most studies were of poor quality and benefit was inconsistent. However, massage for mechanical neck disorders appears to provide immediate or short-term effectiveness for pain and tenderness.

Cervical orthotic use has no definitive supporting evidence after whiplash injuries, but a single trial showed that short-term immobilization was effective for cervical radiculopathy. Potential complications of cervical orthoses include pressure-induced skin injury and dysphagia. Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found act-as-usual was more effective for reducing pain intensity than use of a soft cervical collar following whiplash injury; no studies reported on disability.
Authors of a systematic review found that aquatic therapy improved quality of life, reduced pain and disability, and improved functional capacity in patients with neck pain.

Therapeutic ultrasound combined with other treatments may improve pain and appears to reduce disability and improve quality of life based on a meta-analysis of 7 RCTs with 449 patients with neck pain. A meta-analysis of 5 additional studies (256 patients with neck pain) that compared therapeutic ultrasound with sham or no treatment demonstrated a significant effect on reduced pain intensity. No adverse events of therapeutic ultrasound were reported.

High-intensity laser therapy was found effective for pain in musculoskeletal disorders, with the highest mean difference for neck pain in a meta-analysis of 12 RCTs. Authors of a meta-analysis of 8 RCTs of high-intensity laser therapy for neck pain concluded that pain intensity and range of motion improved based on low to moderate quality evidence but not function. Findings from another meta-analysis including 20 RCTs concurred, with only the results for pain intensity reaching the minimal clinically important difference reported in the literature.

In a meta-analysis of 16 small trials, low-level laser therapy was effective in treating patients with acute and chronic neck pain (NNT = 2 for global improvement; 95% CI, 1-3).Similarly, pooled results revealed that low-level laser therapy was effective for pain reduction and range of motion but not for disability improvement based on a meta-analysis of 13 RCTs with 556 patients with myofascial neck pain.

In a RCT of 120 patients with radicular pain from cervical spinal stenosis or cervical herniated disc, both ultrasound-guided selective nerve root block and fluoroscopy-guided transforaminal epidural block resulted in significant improvements in function and pain. Five patients in the fluoroscopy group received inadvertent intravascular injections that might have been averted with use of ultrasound guidance.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found similar benefit on pain and function with cervical epidural injections of local anesthetic alone or with a steroid in the management of neck pain at both 6 and 12 months.
There were no significant differences between epidural nonsteroid and nonepidural injections for positive outcomes or pain reduction, based on limited direct comparisons.

Cochrane authors found little or no evidence of benefit from electrotherapy approaches. However, in an RCT of 124 patients with cervical spondylosis, those receiving percutaneous neuromuscular electrical stimulation exhibited a greater decrease in mean pain scores on a VAS and neck disability index than patients receiving a sham procedure at the end of the 12-week treatment and at 4-week follow-up.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 5 studies found low-level evidence that focused extracorporeal shock wave therapy was effective for short-term relief of neck pain in patients with myofascial pain syndrome. Similarly, authors of a meta-analysis of 11 RCTs of patients with myofascial pain syndrome in the neck and shoulder found extracorporeal shock wave therapy improved pain intensity but not disability compared to other treatments.
In an RCT of 320 patients with cervical spondylosis, extracorporeal shock wave therapy compared to sham therapy was more effective for improved post-treatment VAS and NDI scores, and range of motion.

MgSO4 iontophoresis and high-power ultrasound were both effective over conventional therapy in decreasing pain and improving neck function in an RCT including 75 physical therapy students with mechanical neck pain who had active myofascial trigger points in the upper trapezius.

Approximately half (48%) of both children and adults with neck pain will report neck pain at the same severity 1 year later. Neck pain resolves more frequently in men than in women and in younger and older-aged patients than in middle-aged patients. Unfortunately, over 50% of people with neck pain do not experience a complete resolution of symptoms. B

Similarly, in a cohort study of 181 adults with a new episode of nonspecific neck pain, just over half reported complete recovery in three months. Faster recovery was independently associated with better self-rated general health, shorter symptom duration, being a smoker, and absence of concomitant upper back pain or headache.

Using a Dutch database of adult primary care patients with nonspecific neck pain, investigators identified nine variables predicting persistent pain at 6 months including age, accompanying low back pain and/or headache, traumatic cause, health status, paid employment, previous neck complaints, pain radiation to elbow/shoulder, and pain intensity.

In another study of patients receiving physical therapy for a primary report of knee, shoulder, back, or neck pain, among the 279 (63.4% of the original sample) with data at 12 months, persistent pain, observed in 36.2%, was associated with having more comorbidities and higher baseline scores on the numerical pain rating scale and the Optimal Screening for Prediction of Referral and Outcome tool for review of systems and yellow flags.

In a systematic review, weighted mean score of idiopathic neck pain (initially rated 64/100) remained high at one year (42/100; 95% CI, 39-45). Disability score, initially 30/100 decreased to 17 (95% CI, 15-19) by 6.5 weeks but then remained without further improvement at one year. A
Whiplash has a poorer prognosis than nontraumatic neck pain, with up to 40% of patients reporting long-term pain. B

In a Canadian cohort study of patients with whiplash-associated disorders, age, number of days to reporting the collision, neck or low back pain intensity, pain other than the neck and back, headache before collision and recovery expectations predicted recovery.

cell.label: Patient presents with neck pain. Recent trauma?

Apply the Canadian C-spine rule. Injury with a dangerous mechanism (eg, fall from 3 ft or more or 5 stairs, diving, motor vehicle collision at >100 km/hr, rollover or ejection, or collision involving a motorized recreational vehicle or a bicycle)?
Stabilize neck; transport for immediate x-ray.

Can you safely assess range of motion of the neck (eg, simple rear-end motor vehicle collision, sitting in the office or ED, ambulatory since the injury, delayed onset of neck pain, or no midline cervical spine tenderness)?
Able to actively rotate the neck 45 degrees left and right?
No immediate x-ray needed. If pain continues, continue the evaluation.
Risk factors for fracture (eg, age 65 years or older, history of or risk factors for cancer, unexplained weight loss, or Paget's disease)?
Consider cancer: order neck x-ray and ESR.
Risk factors for infection (eg, immunosuppression, previous spine surgery, history of IV drug use, or prolonged steroid use)?
Consider osteomyelitis or septic arthritis: order CBC, ESR, white blood cell labeled bone scan, and MRI.
Weakness, numbness, and paresthesias of the arms? Reduced deep tendon reflexes?
Consider cervical disc herniation: order MRI (17% of people without symptoms have a disc herniation, so interpret with caution).
Other neurologic signs (eg, bowel or bladder dysfunction, clonus, Babinski sign, spasticity, gait disturbance, or electric shocks down the back and legs on neck flexion [Lhermitte sign])?
Consider arthritis: order x-rays, ESR, and rheumatoid factor.
Consider nonspecific neck pain without radiculopathy, cervical strain, myofascial syndrome, muscle spasm, or cervical spondylosis.
